item.title: The Gold Guide: the rulebook for medical training
item.description:
Kate and Tom take apart the Gold Guide, COPMeD's reference guide for postgraduate foundation and specialty training across the UK, now in its 11th edition (5 August 2026, corrected 15 September 2026). What it is and isn't (not law, not a contract, but the source of training numbers, ARCP outcomes and appeal rights), who does what (Dean, TPD, Educational and Clinical Supervisors, colleges, employer), the trainee's journey through Form R, less than full time, the 14-day rule and out of programme, how an ARCP panel works and what each outcome means, reviews and appeals, the Tattersall judicial review, and what the Medical Training Review in England might change.

Take-home points

  • The Gold Guide is not legislation and not contractual, but the High Court (Tattersall v NHS England, 2023) held that the right of appeal arises from it alone, so decisions under it must be lawful, reasonable and fair and are open to judicial review.
  • The Postgraduate Dean, not the trust medical director, is the Responsible Officer for doctors in training from F2 onwards; the 15 September 2026 correction to the 11th edition was about exactly this.
  • ARCP is a documentary review held in absentia by a panel of at least three, with college external advisers and lay representation. Outcome 2 means catch up without extra time, 3 means extra time, 4 means release, 5 means the evidence is missing. Non-standard outcomes should never surprise the trainee.
  • The practical numbers: 10 working days to request a review or appeal; 14 days' absence in a year triggers a CCT-date review; LTFT is normally no lower than 50% (never below 20%); out of programme needs six months' notice and normally a year in post first.
  • The guide is reviewed every two years. Phase 2 of the Medical Training Review in England (independent chair Jane Dacre, eight working groups, proposals due by April 2027) may drive bigger changes, but nothing from it is in force.

Key sources

  • COPMeD: Gold Guide 11th edition (5 August 2026, updated 15 September 2026)

item.title: Rock through the ages: genres and the bands that made them
item.description:
Kate and Tom race through seventy-odd years of rock, genre by genre, with a record or two for each stop: from Sister Rosetta Tharpe and fifties rock and roll, through the British Invasion, psychedelia, heavy metal, prog, glam, punk, post-punk and goth, to grunge, Britpop, the 2000s guitar revival and today's post-punk bands, with a running thread on Leeds and Sheffield.

Take-home points

  • Rock grew out of Black American gospel, blues and R&B; Sister Rosetta Tharpe was playing loud electric guitar in 1944.
  • British bands played American records back to America, and that loop runs through the whole story.
  • Most new genres are a reaction: when something gets too big, long or polished, the next lot strips it back.
  • Leeds matters: Gang of Four, the Mekons, the Sisters of Mercy, Kaiser Chiefs and Yard Act.
  • Starter playlist: Johnny B. Goode, You Really Got Me, Purple Haze, Paranoid, Anarchy in the UK, Damaged Goods, Smells Like Teen Spirit, Common People, I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor, and a Yard Act track.

Key sources

  • Strange Things Happening Every Day
  • Black Sabbath (album)
  • Music in Leeds
  • Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not
  • Yard Act

item.title: How NHS money flows: from Treasury to trust
item.description:
Kate and Tom follow NHS money in England from the Spending Review to the Department of Health, through integrated care boards, to how a trust is actually paid under the NHS Payment Scheme, and why deficits, cost improvement programmes and the end of system breakeven now bite at trust level. Includes the Health Bill to abolish NHS England, which has passed the Commons and had its Lords second reading on 13 October 2026, and is not yet law.

Take-home points

  • Elective work is paid per case at the full national price; adult critical care sits in the fixed block, so argue for ICU capacity in terms of protected elective lists.
  • The 2026/27 tariff assumes 2% efficiency a year (cost uplift initially 2.03%, efficiency factor 2.0%), which is where CIPs come from.
  • Since 1 April 2026 each trust must break even on its own; deficit support is about £1.3bn this year, down from £2.2bn, and tapering.
  • NHS England's abolition is not law yet: the Bill would let the Secretary of State cap trust spending, remove foundation trust status and appoint FT boards.
  • Medical bank spend was the main driver of the Q1 2026/27 provider overspend.

Key sources

  • Spending Review 2025 (HM Treasury)
